notes.short: “Blessed” six times, over every part of life
notes.about: In Hebrew each of the six clauses in these verses begins with the word “blessed.” Town and country, children, crops and herds, basket and bowl, coming in and going out: the repeated word spreads the blessing over every part of an obedient Israel's life. Verses 16 to 19 answer with “cursed.”

lines.words: You will be blessed in the city
The fruit of your womb will be blessed, as well as the produce of your land and the offspring of your livestock— the calves of your herds and the lambs of your flocks.
Your basket and kneading bowl will be blessed.
You will be blessed when you come in
and blessed when you go out.

original.note: In Hebrew each of the six clauses opens with barukh, “blessed” (twice as “and blessed”); in verses 4 and 5 the BSB puts the word later in the sentence.

notes.evidence: Bullinger gives these verses as an example of Anaphora, and says verses 16 to 19 repeat “cursed” at the start of each sentence in the same way. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the fulness of God's blessing in all of life is pictured by the sixfold repetition of “blessed”; T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) says its six repetitions bring in the forms the blessing would take.

cites.quote: See the same figure in verses 16-19 with the word “ cursed ” repeated at the beginning of successive sentences.

cites.quote: In Deu 28:3-6, the fulness of the blessing of God in all the relations of life is depicted in a sixfold repetition of the word "blessed." Israel will be blessed in the town and in the field, the two spheres in which its life moves

notes.short: The basket and bowl stand for what they hold
notes.about: The blessing is spoken over a basket and a kneading bowl, but the vessels stand for what fills them: the basket for the seed or the fruit gathered in it, and the bowl for the meal, or all that is stored and made ready to eat. On one reading the pair spans the work from first to last.

figure.name: Metonymy
figure.part: of the Subject: the container for the contents
figure.means: what the vessels hold: the seed or the fruit gathered in the basket, and the meal or store kept in the bowl

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Metonymy of the Subject, the container put for its contents, and takes the basket, probably, for the seed and the kneading trough for the meal, the start and finish of their work. Clarke takes the basket for the olive gathering and vintage it was used to collect, and the store for all that is laid up or made ready to eat.
notes.limit: The writers differ on what the basket held, seed or gathered fruit, and some take the two as the very vessels, used to carry things on a journey.

cites.quote: The container is put for the contents. Here, probably, the “basket” is put for the seed, and “kneading-trough” for the meal; the beginning and the end of their labours.

cites.quote: Thy basket - Thy olive gathering and vintage, as the basket was employed to collect those fruits. Store - משארת mishereth, kneading-trough, or remainder; all that is laid up for future use, as well as what is prepared for present consumption.

notes.short: Moses calls on the heavens and earth to listen
notes.about: Moses opens his song by turning from the people to call on the heavens and the earth to listen. The call marks how weighty the song is. Many read them as called to stand witness, as Moses said he would “call heaven and earth to witness against them” (31:28). Isaiah 1:2 opens the same way.

figure.name: Apostrophe
figure.words: Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; hear, O earth
figure.means: Moses turns from the people to address the heavens and the earth as if they could hear, to mark how weighty his song is

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Apostrophe to inanimate things, the song's solemn opening. Calvin says Moses turns to address heaven and earth as witnesses, though they lack understanding, as Isaiah does. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says Moses summons them to hearken; T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) says they are invoked to show the weight of what follows; Henry calls it a solemn appeal, as in 31:28.
notes.limit: Some take the heavens and the earth to stand for those who live in them, angels and men; others take them as the heavens and the earth themselves, called to listen as witnesses.

cites.quote: Thus solemnly and emphatically opens this “Song of Moses” (which describes the whole history of Israel from the beginning to the end) and call us to give our attention to it and to consider it.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: heaven and earth would be witnesses of their prodigious obtuseness; nay, he turns and addresses himself to heaven and earth, and thus signifies that it was worthy of the attention of all creatures, even although they were without intelligence or feeling ... just as Isaiah ... in like manner appeals to the heavens and the earth
Moses summons heaven and earth to hearken to his words, because the instruction which he was about to proclaim concerned both heaven and earth, i.e., the whole universe.

notes.short: Walls “up to the heavens”: very high walls
notes.about: The people repeat the spies' report of cities “with walls up to the heavens.” The words say more than is literally meant, to stress how high the walls stood. Moses uses the same picture in 9:1, so the walls were truly great; but told this way, the report made the people's hearts melt.

figure.name: Hyperbole
figure.means: walls of great height, too high, it seemed, to be taken

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the words under Hyperbole, as expressing the cities' great height. Benson calls them a hyperbole for very high walls, which Moses grants in 9:1; Henry, a hyperbole the spies used to dishearten the people.
notes.limit: Some do not take the words as an overstatement but as a true account of how high the towns looked to those who saw them.

cites.quote: “The cities are great, and walled up to heaven,” to express their great height. So Deu 9:1, etc.

notes.short: “Teach them diligently”: in Hebrew, whet them
notes.about: The words “teach them diligently” render a Hebrew word that means to whet or sharpen. Read so, God's words are to be taught to children so that they go deep within. Some read in it also teaching given again and again, which can be pictured as a knife turned on each side in whetting.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.means: whet or sharpen them: teach them so that, like a sharp point, they go deep into heart and mind

original.note: In Hebrew “teach them diligently” is one word, from shanan, to whet or sharpen, the word used of a sword in Deuteronomy 32:41.

notes.evidence: Poole says the Hebrew is whet or sharpen them, to pierce deep into the heart, and calls it a metaphor for teaching diligently, earnestly and often. Henry takes up the reading whet them: repeat the words so they pierce the heart, as a knife is turned on each side in whetting. Calvin says the word properly means to whet, not to repeat: the teaching is to pierce the mind like a sword's point.
notes.limit: The picture is in the Hebrew word only; the BSB gives its sense. The writers differ on whether it also means teaching often repeated: one sets that sense aside and keeps only teaching that pierces the mind.

cites.quote: Heb. whet, or sharpen them, so as they may pierce deep into their hearts. This metaphor signifies the manner of instructing them, that it is to be done diligently, earnestly, frequently, discreetly, and dexterously.

Thou shalt whet them diligently upon thy children, so some read it; frequently repeat these things to them, try all ways of instilling them into their minds, and making them pierce into their hearts; as, in whetting a knife, it is turned first on this side, then on that. ... Be careful and exact in teaching thy children; and aim, as by whetting, to sharpen them, and put an edge upon them.

The word שנן shanan, which Moses uses, means properly “to whet.” Commentators think that it is employed metaphorically for “to reiterate,” or “to repeat constantly,” ... its signification may be transitive, viz., that they should cause it to penetrate their minds, as if they should prick them with the point of a sword; for the other translation does not seem consistent.

notes.short: Arrows and sword, then blood and heads, in turn
notes.about: Four lines take turns. The third line goes back to the first, the arrows made drunk with blood. The fourth goes back to the second, the sword that devours flesh.

lines.words: I will make My arrows drunk with blood,
the blood of the slain and captives,
the heads of the enemy leaders.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse as one of two four-line passages whose latter lines are to be referred in turn to the former. Bullinger, under Alternate: the a lines relate to the arrows, the b lines to the sword.

cites.quote: Those which consist of four lines generally form two regular distichs; but there is sometimes a peculiar artifice to be perceived in the distribution of the sentences ... In both the above passages, the latter members are to be alternately referred to the former.
